messages.subject: Re: manual selection as MSImage
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You would then do:

my_msset2 <- my_msset[,my_selection]

to make a subsetted MSImageSet using the selected pixels.

The select() method returns a logical vector of the selected pixels instead of an MSImageSet because there are more ways one might want to use the selection besides creating a new MSImageSet, such as using it as the response in fitting a statistical model.

Kyle

messages.subject: Re: plot mean spectra
messages.body_plain:
In this case, it is not an ordinary R command.

By default, if you give the Cardinal versions of plot() or image() multiple pixels or features, then it will take the mean over them. So by default, if you give all of the pixels to the plot() method, Cardinal will take the mean spectrum over them. (You can provide a function to the 'fun' argument to take, for example, a max or median spectrum.)

Note that this behaves differently if you provide the 'coord' or 'mz' arguments rather than 'pixel' or 'feature'. If you provide the 'coord' or 'mz' arguments, then the default is to plot them separately rather than average over them. This is to make it easier to give a list of specific m/z values you want plotted separately. This behavior can be changed using the 'pixel.groups' and 'feature.groups' arguments. (Pixels and features in the same group will be averaged over; those in different groups will be plotted separately.)

Thanks, Hussam!

-Kyle

messages.subject: Re: plotting 3D images
messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your comments, Heath!

I am not sure of one that can plot images of data from a non-regular grid. Especially if they use rasters, most designed specifically for images expect a regular grid.

However, it occurs to me that my implementation for 3D plotting doesn't rely on rasters, and with some tweaking would work for data on non-regular grid.

This is done using the trans3d() function with points() after calling persp(), to plot a cloud of points. The same can be accomplished with cloud() in lattice. The 'rgl' package also has interactive implementations. For 3D, you're not longer rastering flat images, so a lot more is possible (as the expense of much slower plotting).

-Kyle

messages.subject: Re: Peak picking and alignment
messages.body_plain:
Hi Denis,

You can get a list of all the peaks' m/z values and intensities for each pixel from a peak-picked dataset by doing:

pData(mzData(imageData(object))) # list of m/z values of peaks at each pixel
pData(peakData(imageData(object))) # list of intensities of peaks at each pixel

To use known peaks, just create a vector of the known m/z values for the peaks, and use it for the 'ref' parameter in peakAlign, e.g.:

mypeaks <- c(187, 535, 2000, 4363, 5000) # m/z values of known peaks
mydataset2 <- peakAlign(mydataset, ref=mypeaks)

(When there is no 'ref', Cardinal just creates it automatically from the local maxima of the mean spectrum.)

Hope this helps!

-Kyle

messages.subject: Re: Classify an unknown tissue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Edu,

The default is to overlay the probabilities for each class using transparency, but if the probabilities for each class are very close and uncertain, then the image can come out muddled and gray.

Try adding 'mode="classes"' to image() so you have:

image (myPrediction, model=list(r=2, s=12), mode="classes", layout=c(2,1), main="MyPrediction")

which will give the "hard" predictions rather than "soft" predictions.

You can extract the pixel-by-pixel probabilities (and predicted classes) directly with

myPrediction[[r=2, s=12]]$probabilities # predicted probabilities of each class
myPrediction[[r=2, s=12]]$classes # predicted class (highest probability)

to see how close the probabilities are.

Hope this helps.

-Kyle
